$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-24).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-24| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}T-24 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-24 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-24 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =24+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}186 & =24+K{e}^{0} \\ 186 & =24+K \\ K & =162\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=24+162{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $3$ minutes, the temperature of the pork leg is ${150}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(3)=150,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred into the ${28}^{∘}C$ water bath.*

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=100,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 100 & =28+K \\ K & =72\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+72{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${67}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=67,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}67 & =28+72{e}^{-10k} \\ 39 & =72{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{13}{24} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{13}{24}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{13}{24})\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =57 \\ 28+72{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =57 \\ 72{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =29 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{29}{72} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{29}{72}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{29}{72}).\end{aligned}

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={34}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-34).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-34} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-34} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-34| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-34>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-34 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-34 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-34 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =34+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${81}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=81,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}81 & =34+K{e}^{0} \\ 81 & =34+K \\ K & =47\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=34+47{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $2$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${65}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(2)=65,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}65 & =34+47{e}^{-2k} \\ 31 & =47{e}^{-2k} \\ \frac{31}{47} & ={e}^{-2k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{31}{47}) & =-2k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{31}{47})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${46}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =46 \\ 34+47{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =46 \\ 47{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =12 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{12}{47} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{12}{47}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{12}{47}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${46}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{12}{47})}{-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{31}{47})}≈7\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.
